name: Android Platform Fluency
description: Governs all platform-specific design decisions for modern Android applications. Use this skill whenever the user asks about Material Design 3 (M3) components, dynamic color, tonal elevation, typography scales, Android navigation patterns (Bottom Navigation vs Rail), edge-to-edge layouts (WindowInsets), adaptive UI (WindowSizeClass), predictive back gestures, or Android accessibility standards like minimum touch targets.

rules.rule: Map all interface colors to the M3 token roles rather than absolute values. Use `Primary` for the most prominent actions, `Secondary` for less prominent elements, `Tertiary` for contrasting accents, `Error` for destructive actions, and `Surface` for backgrounds.
rules.why: Hardcoding hex colors breaks user-generated Dynamic Color (Material You) and makes dark mode implementation rigid and brittle.
rules.check: Are you defining a color by its hex code instead of its semantic M3 role?
rules.bad: `background-color: #6200EE`
rules.good: `background-color: colorPrimary` or `MaterialTheme.colorScheme.primary`

rules.rule: Every container color must be paired with its specific "On" color token for text and iconography (e.g., `Primary` container must use `On Primary` text; `Surface` must use `On Surface`).
rules.why: The "On" color tokens are mathematically calculated by the M3 palette generator to guarantee accessible contrast ratios against their parent containers in both light and dark modes.
rules.check: Is the text color inside a `Primary` button explicitly set to `On Primary`?
rules.bad: Setting the text color of a `Primary` button to `#FFFFFF` manually.
rules.good: Setting the text color of a `Primary` button to `MaterialTheme.colorScheme.onPrimary`.

rules.rule: Use M3 Tonal Elevation (shifting the background color slightly lighter or darker) to differentiate overlapping surfaces, reserving heavy drop shadows exclusively for transient elements like Modals, FABs, and Dialogs.
rules.why: M3 modernizes the UI by flattening the visual hierarchy. Overusing drop shadows creates a cluttered, outdated "Material Design 1" look.
rules.check: Are you using a drop shadow to separate a permanent list item from its background?
rules.bad: Adding an 8dp drop shadow to every card in a scrolling feed.
rules.good: Applying Elevation Level 1 (a subtle tonal shift) to the cards, and keeping them shadowless until dragged.

rules.rule: Strictly utilize the 5 standard M3 typography categories: `Display` (massive, short text), `Headline` (primary page titles), `Title` (medium emphasis, app bars), `Body` (long-form reading), and `Label` (buttons, tiny metadata).
rules.why: Deviating from the scale breaks typographic rhythm and accessibility scaling.
rules.check: Can every text element on the screen be mapped cleanly to one of the 5 M3 type roles?
rules.bad: Creating a custom "Subtext_Mini_Bold" style at 11sp.
rules.good: Using `Label Small` for the timestamp on a message.

rules.rule: Every interactive element must have a minimum clickable area of 48x48dp, regardless of the visual size of the component itself.
rules.why: 48dp translates to roughly 9mm, the minimum physical size required for a human finger to reliably tap without error.
rules.check: Is the bounding box of the click listener at least 48x48dp, even if the icon inside is only 24x24dp?
rules.bad: A 24x24dp close icon with exactly a 24x24dp touch target.
rules.good: A 24x24dp close icon with 12dp of invisible padding on all sides, resulting in a 48x48dp touch target.

rules.rule: Use `Filled Buttons` for the single highest priority action on screen, `Tonal Buttons` for high-priority secondary actions, `Outlined Buttons` for medium priority, and `Text Buttons` for the lowest priority actions.
rules.why: Providing multiple `Filled Buttons` confuses the user about what the primary goal of the screen is.
rules.check: Is there more than one `Filled Button` visible in the immediate viewport?
rules.bad: A dialog with a Filled "Cancel" button and a Filled "Submit" button.
rules.good: A dialog with a Text "Cancel" button and a Filled "Submit" button.

rules.rule: M3 Buttons must use fully rounded pill-shapes (Corner size: 100%) by default, contain label text using the `Label Large` type token, and optionally include an 18x18dp icon placed before the text.
rules.why: Standardizing button anatomy ensures users instantly recognize interactive elements across the OS.
rules.check: Are the buttons fully rounded, and is the text capitalized normally (M3) rather than ALL CAPS (M2)?
rules.bad: A rectangular button with ALL CAPS text.
rules.good: A pill-shaped button with Sentence case text.

rules.rule: Use a FAB exclusively for the single most common, primary action in the current screen context. Place it in the bottom-right corner, 16dp from the edges.
rules.why: The FAB is the most visually prominent element on the screen. Using it for a secondary action wastes its visual weight.
rules.check: Does the action the FAB performs represent the main reason the user is on this screen?
rules.bad: Using a FAB to open the settings menu on a social feed.
rules.good: Using a FAB to "Compose New Tweet" on a social feed.

rules.rule: Use `Filled TextFields` for forms with multiple inputs to establish a clear visual baseline, and use `Outlined TextFields` in isolated contexts or where a filled background conflicts with the surface.
rules.why: M3 explicitly defines these two styles to solve different spatial problems. Filled is for dense forms; Outlined is for focus.
rules.check: Are you mixing Filled and Outlined text fields in the same form?
rules.bad: A login form where "Email" is an Outlined field and "Password" is a Filled field.
rules.good: A login form where both fields are Filled, providing a consistent vertical rhythm.

rules.rule: Differentiate cards by choosing one of the three M3 types: `Elevated Card` (uses a drop shadow, best for distinct items), `Filled Card` (uses a surface variant color, best for grouping), or `Outlined Card` (uses a border, best for subtle boundaries).
rules.why: Mixing card styles inappropriately creates visual chaos.
rules.check: Does the card style match its level of interactivity and importance?
rules.bad: Using an Outlined Card for a highly interactive, draggable item.
rules.good: Using an Elevated Card for a draggable item, and Filled Cards for static dashboard widgets.

rules.rule: Use a Bottom Navigation Bar only for top-level destinations, containing exactly 3 to 5 items. Never use it for actions (like "Compose" or "Search").
rules.why: The Bottom Nav is for structural movement. Placing actions in the nav bar conflates navigation with execution.
rules.check: Does every icon in the Bottom Nav change the entire view of the application?
rules.bad: A Bottom Nav with "Home", "Profile", and a "Create Post" action.
rules.good: A Bottom Nav with "Home", "Search", "Notifications", and "Profile".

rules.rule: Automatically convert Bottom Navigation Bars into a vertical Navigation Rail on the left edge of the screen when the layout expands to Tablet/Foldable sizes (Compact to Medium/Expanded WindowSizeClass).
rules.why: Bottom Navigation stretches uncomfortably on wide screens and is ergonomically difficult to reach on tablets. The left rail maps perfectly to where the user's left thumb rests holding a tablet.
rules.check: If the screen width exceeds 600dp, does the navigation move to the left edge?
rules.bad: A 10-inch tablet layout where the Bottom Nav stretches across the entire bottom edge.
rules.good: A tablet layout utilizing a Navigation Rail on the left, leaving the bottom edge clean.

rules.rule: Use a modal Navigation Drawer (hamburger menu) only when the app has more than 5 top-level destinations, or requires deep hierarchical navigation that cannot fit in a Bottom Nav.
rules.why: Items in a drawer are hidden (out of sight, out of mind). Hiding primary destinations reduces engagement.
rules.check: Could these destinations fit comfortably in a Bottom Nav or Rail?
rules.bad: Hiding the 3 main features of the app inside a hamburger menu to make the UI look "clean".
rules.good: Using a Bottom Nav for the 4 main features, and a Navigation Drawer for "Settings, Help, About, and Account Management".

rules.rule: The app's root layout must draw entirely under the transparent system status bar (top) and navigation bar (bottom). Use `WindowInsets` to apply internal padding so interactive content is not obscured.
rules.why: Modern Android requires edge-to-edge drawing to prevent ugly black bars at the top and bottom of the screen, providing an immersive experience.
rules.check: Are lists capable of scrolling *behind* the translucent bottom navigation handle?
rules.bad: Setting the system navigation bar to solid black.
rules.good: Drawing the UI behind a transparent navigation bar and applying `navigationBarsPadding()` to the bottom-most button.

rules.rule: Never place interactive elements (like FABs or Bottom Navs) within the system gesture zones (bottom inset or side insets). Always add inset padding.
rules.why: Placing a button in the system navigation zone means the user will accidentally trigger the Android Home or Back gesture when trying to click the button.
rules.check: Is the FAB padded above the bottom WindowInset?
rules.bad: A FAB sitting flush against the very bottom pixels of the physical screen.
rules.good: A FAB sitting 16dp above the `systemGestureInsets.bottom`.

rules.rule: Ensure custom views, dialogs, and navigation frameworks support the Android Predictive Back gesture, allowing the user to peek at the previous screen before committing to the back action.
rules.why: Android 14+ makes the back gesture predictive. Apps that manually intercept the back button without providing the predictive animation feel broken and trap the user.
rules.check: Does swiping from the left edge slowly reveal the previous screen or home screen?
rules.bad: Intercepting the hardware back button with `onBackPressed()` to show a custom modal without registering an `OnBackPresse
rules.good: Using the standard AndroidX Navigation component which handles predictive back animations automatically.

rules.rule: Design layouts to react to three breakpoints: `Compact` (Phones, <600dp), `Medium` (Foldables/Small Tablets, 600-840dp), and `Expanded` (Large Tablets, >840dp).
rules.why: Hardcoding specific dp widths guarantees the UI will break on the diverse ecosystem of Android devices.
rules.check: Does the layout fundamentally restructure (not just stretch) when moved from Compact to Expanded?
rules.bad: A single column list that stretches to 1000dp wide on a tablet.
rules.good: A single column list on Compact that transforms into a two-pane List-Detail view on Expanded.

rules.rule: When transitioning from Compact to Expanded width, convert deep list-to-detail navigation flows into a side-by-side Two-Pane layout (List on left, Detail on right).
rules.why: Forcing users to navigate back and forth on a large screen wastes space and requires excessive interaction cost.
rules.check: Does the app utilize the extra horizontal space to show hierarchy?
rules.bad: A tablet app where clicking an email opens a new full-screen window, requiring the user to hit "Back" to see the inbox a
rules.good: A tablet app where clicking an email in the left pane updates the reading pane on the right.

rules.rule: Dialogs must never stretch to the edges of the screen. They must have a minimum margin of 24dp from the left and right edges, and a maximum width of 560dp.
rules.why: Full-width dialogs look like entirely new screens, confusing the user's mental model of the back stack.
rules.check: Is the dialog constrained to a readable maximum width on tablets?
rules.bad: A dialog that stretches to 1000dp wide on a tablet, making the text impossible to track.
rules.good: A dialog centered on the tablet screen capped at 560dp wide.

rules.rule: Use Snackbars for brief, low-priority feedback about an operation. They must appear at the bottom of the screen, sit *above* bottom navigation bars, and disappear automatically (usually 4-10 seconds).
rules.why: Snackbars are transient and should not permanently obscure UI. Placing them under a FAB or Navigation Bar makes them illegible.
rules.check: If a Snackbar appears, does it push the FAB up or sit cleanly above the Bottom Nav?
rules.bad: A Snackbar that appears at the very bottom edge of the screen, underneath the Bottom Navigation bar.
rules.good: A Snackbar that appears immediately above the Bottom Navigation bar, temporarily shifting the FAB upward.

rules.rule: Use the standard M3 shape scales: `None` (0dp), `Extra Small` (4dp), `Small` (8dp), `Medium` (12dp), `Large` (16dp), `Extra Large` (28dp), and `Full` (Pill). Do not use arbitrary radii like 7dp or 11dp.
rules.why: Consistent corner radii create a unified subconscious structural language across the app.
rules.check: Do the corner radii map to the official M3 shape scale?
rules.bad: A card with an arbitrary 13dp border radius.
rules.good: A card using the standard `Medium` (12dp) shape token.

rules.rule: Use a `Switch` to instantly activate/deactivate a standalone setting. Use a `Checkbox` when selecting multiple options from a list or when the selection requires a "Save" button to take effect.
rules.why: A switch implies an immediate system state change (like a light switch). A checkbox implies batching data for future submission.
rules.check: If the user toggles this control, does the setting apply immediately without a save button?
rules.bad: Using checkboxes in a settings menu where toggling them immediately changes the app behavior.
rules.good: Using switches in the settings menu, and checkboxes in a multi-select deletion list.

rules.rule: Dividers must be 1dp thick and use the `Outline Variant` token color to ensure they are subtle and do not command visual hierarchy.
rules.why: Heavy or highly contrasted dividers create visual noise and segment the screen too aggressively.
rules.check: Are dividers barely visible, providing just enough structure to separate content?
rules.bad: A 2dp thick, solid black divider between list items.
rules.good: A 1dp thick divider using `MaterialTheme.colorScheme.outlineVariant`.

rules.rule: When a modal (Dialog, Bottom Sheet, or Navigation Drawer) is open, the background content must be obscured by a Scrim. The M3 standard scrim is the `Scrim` token color (usually pure black) set to 32% opacity.
rules.why: The scrim focuses the user's attention on the modal and disables interaction with the background surface.
rules.check: Does the background dim to exactly 32% opacity when the modal opens?
rules.bad: Opening a dialog over a fully bright background, making it hard to read.
rules.good: The background instantly dims using `colorScheme.scrim` at 32% alpha.  ## Anti-patterns  ### 1. The iOS Port Designing a
